title: Why do other planets have seasons?
subtitle: Planets & orbits
subject: sciences
description: On Earth, the seasons come from the tilt of the axis. Elsewhere the same rule gives winters that last 42 years, or almost no seasons at all.

hero.hook: Our four seasons are the mild case. Elsewhere, one summer can last for decades.

blocks.text: On Earth, summer and winter come mostly from the **tilt** of the axis, about **23.5°**. The Sun beats down harder on one hemisphere, then on the other. The pattern feels obvious to us. In the solar system, it is really the mild version.
Every planet combines its own tilt with the shape of its orbit. The result: worlds with no seasons, others with extreme contrasts, and winters that run for decades.
[[Obliquity]] is the angle between a planet's rotation axis and the perpendicular to its orbit. The bigger that angle, the sharper the seasons.

blocks.caption: Uranus, tilted by about 98°, has extreme seasons that last 42 years

blocks.text: **Uranus** is the extreme case: a tilt of about **98°**, almost lying on its side. It takes **84 years** to go around the Sun. Each pole then gets nearly **42 years** of continuous daylight, followed by **42 years** of total night. **Mars**, at **25.2°**, is much like Earth, but its year lasts **687 Earth days**, so spring and autumn run six months each. **Jupiter** and **Mercury**, almost upright, have virtually no seasons.
On Uranus and Neptune, the extreme pressure may make it “rain” diamonds formed out of carbon from the atmosphere.

sections.title: When distance from the Sun counts too

blocks.text: Earth's orbit is nearly circular, so the distance to the Sun barely changes. Summer and winter do not come from that distance, but from the angle of the rays.

On **Mars**, the orbit is far more oval, more **eccentric**: from **207 to 249 million km**. In the southern hemisphere, summer falls near [[perihelion]], the closest point to the Sun. Summers there are shorter, but hotter. That thermal shock sometimes sets off planet-wide **dust storms** that blot out the sky.
In **2018**, a seasonal Martian storm finished off the Opportunity rover for good by hiding the Sun from it.

**Mercury**, with no real atmosphere and no tilt, lives through **daily** extremes instead: **430°C** in the sunlight, **-180°C** at night. **Venus** spins the other way, in [[Retrograde rotation]] from east to west, and its tilt is extreme, but its monstrous **greenhouse effect** traps heat in the atmosphere and levels the temperature at about **460°C** everywhere, all the time.
**Saturn**, tilted much like Earth, has seasons of about **7 years**. The angle of the [[rings of Saturn]] changes how much light each hemisphere receives, and even shifts the color of the clouds.
On Venus, a single spin of the planet takes longer than one trip around the Sun: **243** Earth days against **225**.

Without the **Moon**, Earth's tilt would swing chaotically between 0° and more than 80° over millions of years. Uranus-style seasons would make the climate almost unlivable. The Moon acts as a **gravitational stabilizer**.
So when astronomers hunt for habitable [[exoplanets]], they also look at how stable the axis is. Mild, regular seasons are not a detail: they are part of what lasting life requires.
Seasons come mostly from the tilt of the axis. On Uranus they last for decades, and on Mars the oval orbit makes them lopsided. On Earth, the Moon keeps them steady.
